bull.argument: Meta's 2025 filing shows a business with strong momentum and cash generation. Total revenue rose 22% to $200.97 billion, and income from operations grew 20% to $83.28 billion. Ad impressions increased 12% and average price per ad rose 9%, indicating that demand for its ads is strengthening alongside reach. Family daily active people reached 3.58 billion, up 7%, and operating cash flow was $115.80 billion. Management also has returned capital, repurchasing $26.26 billion of stock and paying $5.32 billion in dividends, and it raised the quarterly dividend. The filing acknowledges real headwinds: EU consent-model changes, Apple iOS limits on targeting, and heavy Reality Labs losses of about $19.19 billion. Still, the core Family of Apps segment earned a 52% operating margin, and management attributes the price gains largely to better ad performance from its targeting and measurement tools. Investors are weighing a strong advertising engine against large AI and hardware spending, and the reported results support the bull case.

claims.claim: Revenue grew 22% year over year to $200.97 billion, with income from operations up 20%.
claims.quote: Total revenue for 2025 was $200.97 billion, an increase of 22% compared to 2024

claims.claim: Average price per ad rose 9%, which management attributes mostly to improved ad performance from its targeting and measurement tools.
claims.quote: The increase in average price per ad in 2025 was driven by an increase in advertising demand, which we believe is mostly due to ongoing improvements to our ad performance from our ad targeting and measurement tools

claims.claim: Operating cash flow was strong at $115.80 billion, and the company repurchased $26.26 billion of stock.
claims.quote: In 2025, we repurchased and subsequently retired 40 million shares of our Class A common stock for an aggregate amount of $26.26 billion.

bear.argument: The bull case leans on headline growth, but the filing shows that growth is tied to spending and to a revenue base under structural pressure. Capital expenditures reached $72.22 billion, and free cash flow fell to $43.59 billion from $52.10 billion in 2024, even as operating cash flow rose. Management guides to $115 billion to $135 billion of capex in 2026, so the cash conversion that supports the buybacks is being absorbed by infrastructure and AI. Net income fell to $60.46 billion from $62.36 billion, and the effective tax rate jumped to 30% because of a $15.93 billion OBBBA charge. Revenue depends almost entirely on advertising, and the filing says data-signal limits from Apple, GDPR and the DMA have 'negatively impacted' ad budgets and will 'continue to adversely affect' them. The EU less-personalized-ads option may be modified further during appeal. Reality Labs lost $19.19 billion, and management expects 2026 losses to be similar. Price-per-ad gains of 9% are partly offset by impression growth into lower-monetizing regions and Reels, so the quality of growth is weaker than the headline suggests.

claims.claim: Free cash flow declined year over year despite higher operating cash flow, because capital spending rose sharply.
Management expects capital expenditures to rise substantially in 2026 to support AI efforts.
claims.quote: We anticipate making capital expenditures of approximately $115 billion to $135 billion in 2026 to support our AI efforts and core business.

claims.claim: The filing states that data-signal limits have negatively affected ad budgets and will keep doing so.
claims.quote: which has negatively impacted, and we expect will continue to negatively impact, the size of the budgets marketers are willing to commit to us

bull.argument: The bear case is right that spending is rising, but the filing shows the core engine still compounding. Free cash flow was $43.59 billion after $69.69 billion of property and equipment purchases, and operating cash flow rose to $115.80 billion from $91.33 billion. That is a business generating far more cash than it needs to reinvest, which is why it could repurchase $26.26 billion of stock and pay $5.32 billion in dividends while still raising the dividend. The net income dip is largely a tax event: the $15.93 billion OBBBA charge is a one-time item, and management says the effective tax rate would have been 13% absent the valuation allowance charge, with 2026 guided to 13-16%. Operating income still rose 20%, and Family of Apps margin was 52%. On regulation, the filing does describe headwinds, but it also says advertising demand rose and price per ad increased 9%, which management credits mostly to better targeting and measurement. Reality Labs losses are large, yet they are a discrete, disclosed investment, and FoA carries the company.

claims.claim: Operating cash flow rose to $115.80 billion, showing cash generation that funds both capex and capital returns.
claims.quote: Net cash provided by operating activities $ 115,800 $ 91,328 $ 71,113

claims.claim: Absent the valuation allowance charge, the 2025 effective tax rate would have been 13%, so the tax jump reflects a one-time item.
claims.quote: Absent the valuation allowance charge as of the enactment date, our 2025 effective tax rate would have decreased by 17 percentage points to 13%.

claims.claim: Price per ad rose 9% because advertising demand increased, which management attributes mostly to better targeting and measurement tools.
claims.quote: The increase in average price per ad in 2025 was driven by an increase in advertising demand, which we believe is mostly due to ongoing improvements to our ad performance from our ad targeting and measurement tools

bear.argument: The bull rebuttal reads the one-time tax charge too generously. The $15.93 billion OBBBA charge was real cash-earnings damage in Q3 2025, and the 13% rate excluding it is a counterfactual; the reported 30% rate is what shareholders got. Operating cash flow of $115.80 billion is impressive, but the filing says it was 'mostly' absorbed: $69.69 billion went to property and equipment, $18.33 billion to non-marketable equity investments, and $26.26 billion plus $5.32 billion to shareholders. Free cash flow fell 16%, and the filing guides capex to $115 to $135 billion in 2026, which will compress FCF further unless operating cash flow grows at a similar pace. Buybacks are being funded partly by a $29.91 billion debt issuance, and long-term debt reached $58.74 billion. On the ad engine, price per ad rose 9%, but management concedes it cannot quantify how much each trend hit revenue, and it says data-signal limits will 'continue to adversely affect' the business 'for the foreseeable future.' The bull case assumes that better targeting offsets these losses; the filing does not show that. Reality Labs losing $19.19 billion, with a similar loss expected in 2026, is not a discrete cost but a recurring drain.

claims.claim: Free cash flow fell year over year, and the filing guides to much higher capital spending in 2026.
claims.quote: We anticipate making capital expenditures of approximately $115 billion to $135 billion in 2026 to support our AI efforts and core business.

claims.claim: The company funded part of its capital returns with new debt issued in November 2025.
claims.quote: $29.91 billion net proceeds from the issuance of fixed-rate senior unsecured notes (the Notes) in November 2025

claims.claim: Management says the ad headwinds from data-signal limits will continue for the foreseeable future.
claims.quote: will continue to adversely affect our advertising revenue for the foreseeable future

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes, so evidence is comparable. The bear better rebuts the bull's tax-normalization argument by pointing out the reported 30% rate is what shareholders bore, and it ties capex guidance and debt-funded buybacks to a weaker cash-conversion story. The bull's responses are reasonable but lean on the counterfactual 13% rate and do not fully address the 2026 capex compression or the debt funding the bear raised.
